title: Life Insurance Product Development and Pricing

questions.stem: The penalty under NIIRA 2025 for marketing a life insurance product without prior NAICOM approval is:

opts.x: ₦250,000 per policy sold.
₦500,000 per day for each day the unapproved product is marketed.
Suspension of the company's licence with immediate effect.
A written warning for the first offence only.

questions.answer: (B) ₦500,000 per day for each day the unapproved product is marketed.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 establishes a per-day penalty for marketing life insurance products without prior NAICOM approval. The daily accrual structure creates an escalating financial consequence proportional to the duration of non-compliance, an insurer marketing an unapproved product for 60 days accumulates ₦30 million in fines. This structure is a stronger deterrent than a fixed per-policy or one-time penalty, which might be treated as a cost of doing business.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A per-policy fine would create minimal deterrent for a high-volume product launch but excessive liability for a specialist product; the per-day model is more consistently calibrated.
(C) Immediate licence suspension as the first-instance penalty for product approval non-compliance would be disproportionate; NIIRA 2025 reserves suspension for more serious or repeated violations.
(D) A written warning with no financial consequence is the pre-NIIRA 2025 approach that the Act's strengthened enforcement philosophy was designed to replace.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, the policy document must be delivered to the policyholder:

opts.x: Within 5 working days of the policy start date.
Within 30 days of premium receipt.
On or before the policy start date; electronic delivery requires confirmation of receipt.
At the insurer's discretion within the first policy month.

questions.answer: (C) On or before the policy start date; electronic delivery requires confirmation of receipt.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 requires the policy document to be in the policyholder's hands no later than the commencement date of coverage. For electronic delivery (email, WhatsApp, online portal), delivery is deemed effective only when the insurer has confirmation of actual receipt, a read receipt, an affirmative response, or logged portal access. This prevents the gap where coverage has commenced but the policyholder has not yet seen the terms governing their coverage.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 5 working days post-commencement would mean coverage is in force before the policyholder knows the policy terms, directly contrary to NIIRA 2025's consumer protection objective.
(B) 60 days is the claims settlement deadline, not the document delivery requirement. Conflating the two is a common examination error.
(D) 'At the insurer's discretion' describes the pre-NIIRA 2025 practice that the mandatory delivery requirement was introduced to eliminate.

questions.stem: The 'deemed approval' provision in NAICOM's product filing process means:

opts.x: NAICOM automatically approves all products without review.
If NAICOM does not respond within 30 days, the product is treated as approved.
Products may be marketed while under review, subject to later approval.
Only new products require NAICOM approval; amendments are exempt.

questions.answer: (B) If NAICOM does not respond to a product filing within 30 days, the product is treated as approved.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The deemed approval provision prevents NAICOM's processing backlog from indefinitely delaying new product launches. If NAICOM does not issue an approval, rejection, or request for further information within 30 days of receiving a complete product filing, the filing is deemed approved and the insurer may market the product. This creates an incentive for NAICOM to review promptly while also protecting insurers from indefinite regulatory silence.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) NAICOM does review all filings, the deemed approval applies only after the 30-day window expires without a NAICOM decision on a complete filing.
(C) Marketing before approval (even while under review) is prohibited under NIIRA 2025. The 30-day deemed approval only activates after the window passes without a decision.
(D) Material product amendments require NAICOM notification or formal resubmission; they are not categorically exempt from the approval process.

questions.stem: The persistency assumption in a life insurance pricing model specifies:

opts.x: The probability of a policyholder dying in each future policy year.
The rate at which the insurer expects to earn investment returns.
The proportion of policyholders expected to keep their policies in force in each year.
The fixed annual cost of administering each in-force policy.

questions.answer: (C) The proportion of policyholders expected to keep their policies in force in each year.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The persistency assumption models the lapse behaviour of the in-force portfolio, what percentage of policies are expected to remain in force in each future policy year. It is the complement of the lapse rate: if persistency is 82% in year 3, the lapse rate is 18% in year 3. Persistency affects the insurer's future premium income stream, the expected claims cost profile (lapses remove policies from the risk pool), and the expense amortisation calculation. Getting persistency assumptions right is critical to pricing profitability.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The probability of dying in each policy year is the mortality assumption (qx from the EFU Nigerian life table), a separate and distinct actuarial input.
(B) Expected investment returns are the yield assumption, the projected return on the insurer's investment of premium funds. A separate actuarial input.
(D) The fixed annual administration cost per policy is the per-policy renewal expense loading, another separate pricing element from the persistency assumption.

questions.stem: A credit life insurance policy under NIIRA 2025 typically has:

opts.x: A fixed sum assured for the entire loan term.
A reducing sum assured mirroring the outstanding loan balance over the loan term.
A sum assured written by a bank and not an insurance company.
An optional sum assured for all loans regardless of amount.

questions.answer: (B) A reducing sum assured mirroring the outstanding loan balance over the loan term.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Credit life insurance is specifically designed to match the risk profile of a repayment loan: as the borrower repays principal each period, the outstanding balance falls, and so does the required coverage amount. A reducing sum assured (the structure of decreasing term assurance) precisely matches this profile, the insurer's maximum exposure at any point equals the outstanding loan balance. This matching eliminates over-insurance (which would burden the borrower with higher premiums than necessary) and under-insurance (which would leave a residual debt uncovered).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A fixed sum assured would over-insure in the later stages of a repayment loan when the outstanding balance is low, imposing unnecessary premium cost.
(C) Credit life must be underwritten by a NAICOM-licensed life insurer, banks cannot underwrite insurance risk on their own account without a separate insurance licence.
(D) NIIRA 2025 makes credit life mandatory (not optional) for qualifying loans above ₦10 million.

questions.stem:
An actuary is conducting a profit test for a proposed 15-year participating endowment policy. The key assumptions are: investment return 11% p.a.; lapse rate 18% in year 1, 10% in years 2–3, 5% in years 4+; first-year expense ₦35,000 per policy; renewal expense ₦7,000 per policy per year.
(a) Explain why the profit test typically shows a loss in year 1 for this type of product.
(b) A sensitivity analysis shows that if the investment return falls to 8% p.a., the product's IRR falls from 18% to 12%, and the company's hurdle rate is 15%. What are the implications of this sensitivity result, and what actions could the product team take to improve IRR?
(c) What role does the lapse assumption play in this product's profitability, and why might actual lapses differ from the pricing assumption in the Nigerian market?

model.h: Part (a): Why Year-1 Shows a Loss

Life insurance economics are front-loaded on cost and back-loaded on profit recovery. Year-1 losses are structural and expected:

1. Acquisition costs: Initial commission (typically 30–40% of first-year premium), new business set-up costs (underwriting, policy printing, data entry), and the first-year expense of ₦35,000 per policy combine to create a first-year cost that typically exceeds first-year premium income.

2. Initial policy reserve: From day one, the insurer must establish and fund a policy reserve equal to the present value of future benefits less the present value of future premiums. This reserve requires an immediate investment of funds that will only be recovered over the policy's life.

3. First-year lapse: An 18% first-year lapse rate means 18% of policies written generate only one premium payment before lapsing. These lapsed policies contributed their acquisition costs but will contribute no future premiums, creating a drag on the cohort's profitability from the outset.

Conclusion: The year-1 loss is a new business strain that is recovered over years 2–15 as premiums accumulate, investment returns compound, and per-policy expenses fall to the much lower ₦7,000 renewal level.
Part (b): Investment Sensitivity: IRR and Hurdle Rate

At 11% investment return: IRR = 18% > 15% hurdle rate → product is commercially viable.
At 8% investment return: IRR = 12% < 15% hurdle rate → product does not meet the required return threshold.

Implications:
1. The product is materially sensitive to investment return assumptions, a 3% drop in investment return destroys 6% of IRR. This indicates that the product's profitability is substantially dependent on investment performance, not just underwriting.

2. At 8% return, the product should not be launched unless the hurdle rate is reduced (a strategic decision by management), the premium is increased, or the product's expense structure is improved.

3. Product repricing options: Reduce initial commission rate; increase year-1 premium; reduce first-year expense loading (e.g., through digital onboarding reducing per-policy acquisition cost); reduce bonus declaration rate (reducing investment return sensitivity of the with-profit element).

4. Stress testing implication: NIIRA 2025's ORSA framework requires the insurer to stress-test its product portfolio against adverse economic scenarios. A product that does not meet hurdle rate at 8% investment return is a material ORSA stress-test failure that requires management action.
Part (c): Role of the Lapse Assumption

The lapse assumption is critical to profitability for two distinct reasons:

1. Effect on premium income: Each lapse removes future premium income from the expected cash flows. A policy that lapses in year 3 contributes only 3 years of premiums rather than 15, directly reducing expected profit.

2. Effect on acquisition cost recovery: Acquisition costs are incurred upfront but recovered over the policy's life. An early lapse (particularly in year 1 at 18%) means the insurer has paid full acquisition costs but recovers only a fraction of them before the policy terminates. The surrender value paid (if any) may not cover the unrecovered acquisition cost.

Specific Nigerian market considerations:
Actual lapse rates in Nigeria are typically higher than pricing assumptions for several reasons:
• Economic volatility: Sudden income shocks (job loss, medical emergency, naira depreciation) cause immediate premium non-payment.
• Mis-selling: Policies sold to customers who cannot sustain the premiums predictably lapse early.
• Trust deficit: Policyholders who have a negative service experience (delayed response, poor claims stories from others) lapse proactively.

If actual lapses exceed pricing assumptions (i.e., persistency is lower than modelled), the product's IRR will be lower than projected, potentially below the hurdle rate. This creates a systematic profitability risk that the actuary must monitor through the annual actuarial investigation.

questions.stem: Explain the NAICOM product filing process under NIIRA 2025. Describe the contents of an actuarial pricing report as required for a product filing submission. Explain the 30-day deemed-approval provision and the regulatory rationale for it. Discuss the consequences, regulatory and commercial, if an insurer proceeds to market with a product that has been disapproved by NAICOM.

model.h: NAICOM Product Filing Process

NIIRA 2025 requires that no life insurance product may be marketed until NAICOM has approved it. The product approval process:

1. Filing preparation: The insurer prepares a complete product filing package (see below) and submits it to NAICOM's Department of Policy and Research through the NAICOM digital filing portal.

2. NAICOM review: NAICOM's actuarial and product review team assesses the filing against the product approval criteria: Shariah compliance (for Takaful products); actuarial adequacy of pricing; consumer disclosure adequacy; policy wording clarity; and alignment with NIIRA 2025's mandatory provisions (cooling-off period, no-premium-no-cover, claims timeline disclosure).

3. Decision: NAICOM issues one of: (a) formal approval; the product may be marketed from the approval date; (b) request for further information; the insurer must respond within a defined period; (c) disapproval; the product cannot be marketed in its current form. The insurer may modify and resubmit.

4. Deemed approval: If NAICOM does not issue any response within 30 days of receiving a complete filing, the product is deemed approved.
Actuarial Pricing Report Contents

The actuarial pricing report submitted to NAICOM must include:
1. Product description: Benefits structure, eligibility criteria, policy term, premium payment options.
2. Pricing assumptions: Mortality (with reference to the EFU Nigerian life tables or the insurer's own experience tables with justification); lapse rates by policy year; investment return assumptions; expense assumptions (initial and renewal, per policy and as % of premium); inflation assumption for expense escalation.
3. Profit test results: IRR vs hurdle rate; reserve adequacy at each assumed scenario; year-by-year cash flow projection.
4. Sensitivity analysis: Results under adverse investment return, adverse lapse, and adverse mortality scenarios.
5. Actuarial certification: The Statutory Actuary's signed certificate that the pricing is actuarially adequate and the product's benefit structure is as described.
6. Benefit illustrations: Examples of projected policy values for sample age/premium combinations under base and conservative assumptions.
30-Day Deemed Approval: Regulatory Rationale

The deemed approval provision balances two competing regulatory interests:
• Consumer protection: NAICOM must be able to review products before they reach consumers. The review power is substantive, not symbolic.
• Market development: Product innovation requires certainty of timing. An insurer that has invested in product development cannot tolerate indefinite regulatory uncertainty about launch dates. Without the deemed approval mechanism, NAICOM's workload backlog could indefinitely delay product launches without any regulatory consequence.

The 30-day window incentivises NAICOM to review promptly (to avoid deemed approvals of products it might have concerns about) while giving insurers certainty about their launch timeline for well-prepared filings.
Consequences of Marketing a NAICOM-Disapproved Product

Regulatory consequences: The per-day financial penalty under NIIRA 2025 (₦500,000 per day). NAICOM may also: issue a public notice requiring the insurer to cease marketing immediately; require all policyholders to be notified and offered a refund of premiums; refer the matter for criminal prosecution of responsible officers in serious cases.

Commercial consequences: Significant reputational damage if the product launch is publicly identified as unapproved. Existing policyholders who purchased the unapproved product may have grounds to rescind their policies and seek premium refunds. The insurer's relationship with NAICOM will be adversely affected, potentially leading to heightened scrutiny on future product filings.
Part (a): Key Product Design Features

1. Reducing sum assured: The credit life policy must have a sum assured that mirrors the outstanding loan balance at each point. For a ₦10m 24-month term loan, the sum assured begins at ₦10m and reduces each month as principal is repaid.

2. Term matching: Policy term must equal the loan term. A 36-month loan requires a 36-month credit life policy. Mismatching creates coverage gaps.

3. Eligible causes: Death (any cause, after the suicide exclusion period) and, optionally, total and permanent disability. NIIRA 2025 mandates coverage of death, disability is a commercial add-on.

4. Single premium or bundled monthly: For short-term fintech loans, a single premium collected at disbursement (and incorporated into the loan) is operationally simpler than monthly collections. The single premium must comply with NIIRA 2025 disclosure; the borrower must know they are purchasing insurance and at what cost.

5. Lender as beneficiary: The lender is named as beneficiary up to the outstanding loan balance. Any excess (if the sum assured exceeds the outstanding balance at death) may be paid to the borrower's estate.
Part (b): API Integration Mechanics

The embedded credit life model requires real-time data exchange between the fintech's lending platform and the life insurer's PAS:

1. Loan origination trigger: When a qualifying loan is approved in the fintech's system, an API call is sent to the insurer's new business API: {borrower_id, loan_amount, loan_term, disbursement_date, borrower_age, borrower_NIN}.

2. Premium calculation response: The insurer's API calculates the credit life premium for the specific borrower (age-rated, loan amount, loan term) and returns the premium to the fintech within seconds. The premium is bundled into the loan amount.

3. Policy issuance: On loan disbursement, the insurer issues the policy electronically (certificate sent to the borrower's email/WhatsApp) and a loan-linked policy record is created in the PAS.

4. Amortisation schedule integration: The insurer's PAS receives the loan's monthly amortisation schedule, enabling it to track the reducing outstanding balance, the basis for the reducing sum assured at any given point.

5. Claim notification: On borrower death, the lender sends a FNOL (first notification of loss) via API: {policy_id, date_of_death, cause_of_death_brief}. The insurer's claims system creates the claim record and begins the 5-day acknowledgement / 60-day settlement clock.
Part (c): Disclosure Obligations to the Borrower

NIIRA 2025's consumer protection and TCF provisions require clear, fair, and not misleading disclosure:
1. Name of insurer: The borrower must know which NAICOM-licensed insurer is providing the credit life coverage, not just that 'insurance is included.'
2. Premium amount: The exact credit life premium included in the loan must be separately itemised and disclosed before signing.
3. Coverage summary: Plain language explanation of what is and is not covered (death covered; suicide during exclusion period not covered; any specific exclusions).
4. Claims process: How the borrower's beneficiary contacts the insurer if the borrower dies.
5. Consent: NDPA 2023 requires the borrower's explicit consent for their health and personal data to be shared with the insurer for underwriting purposes.
Part (d): Regulatory Requirements for the Insurer

1. NIIRA 2025 life insurance licence: The insurer must hold a valid NAICOM life insurance licence, not an Insurtech Partnering certificate. Only a licensed insurer can bear insurance risk.
2. NAICOM product approval: The credit life product design must be NAICOM-approved before the fintech integration is deployed.
3. Documented partnership agreement: The commercial arrangement between the fintech and the insurer must be documented in a formal agreement disclosed to NAICOM. The insurer remains responsible for regulatory compliance with all policyholders regardless of the fintech's distribution role.
4. NDPA 2023 data processing agreement: A compliant data processing agreement must govern the borrower data shared from the fintech to the insurer for underwriting and claims purposes.

questions.stem: Critically evaluate the significance of the NAICOM product filing and approval regime under NIIRA 2025 for the quality of life insurance products available to Nigerian consumers. In your answer, assess the extent to which the regime addresses the historical problem of misleading benefit illustrations, unsuitable product design, and inadequate pricing; identify any limitations or gaps in the current framework; and propose enhancements that would further strengthen consumer protection while preserving the commercial incentive for product innovation.

model.h: Thesis

NIIRA 2025's product approval regime is the most important regulatory mechanism for ensuring that Nigerian consumers encounter only actuarially sound, consumer-fairly designed, and appropriately priced life insurance products. It directly addresses three historical product quality problems (misleading illustrations, unsuitable design, and inadequate pricing) but it is not without limitations.
Historical Problems the Regime Addresses

1. Misleading benefit illustrations: Before NIIRA 2025's enhanced product approval guidelines, Nigerian life insurers regularly illustrated only the optimistic scenario (high bonus declarations, favourable investment returns) without showing the conservative projection. The updated product approval requirements mandate dual-scenario illustrations, a practice that prevents cherry-picked optimistic projections from driving unsuitable sales decisions.

2. Unsuitable product design: NAICOM's product approval process now requires that each product filing demonstrate the target market for which the product is designed and appropriate. Products with high early surrender penalties, complex benefit triggers, or premium structures that make lapses highly likely in the Nigerian income environment face heightened scrutiny.

3. Inadequate pricing: The actuarial pricing report requirement, with Statutory Actuary certification, creates a formal accountability mechanism for pricing adequacy. An insurer that prices a product inadequately (too cheaply to attract volume) faces the Statutory Actuary's refusal to certify, or subsequent regulatory scrutiny when loss ratios exceed sustainable levels.
Limitations of the Current Framework

1. NAICOM review capacity: NAICOM's product actuarial team is small relative to the volume of product filings from 50+ licensed insurers. The 30-day deemed approval creates pressure on this limited resource; the team must review within 30 days or the product is automatically approved, regardless of quality.

2. Post-approval monitoring: The regime is entirely front-loaded at approval. Once approved, a product can be marketed without NAICOM monitoring actual sales practices, actual benefit illustrations used by agents, or actual persistency outcomes. Post-launch conduct monitoring is largely absent.

3. Amendment triggers are unclear: The boundary between a material product amendment (requiring new NAICOM approval) and a minor administrative change (not requiring approval) is ambiguous, creating inconsistent compliance across the market.

4. No product performance database: NAICOM does not publish product-level claims, lapse, or complaint data that would enable consumers to compare products across insurers. Without this transparency, the product approval certificate is a process compliance indicator, not a performance quality signal.
Proposed Enhancements

1. Post-launch persistency monitoring: Require insurers to report product-level 13-month persistency rates to NAICOM annually. Products with persistency consistently below an industry benchmark trigger NAICOM review of sales practices and suitability assessment compliance.

2. Mystery shopper programme: NAICOM to conduct regular mystery shopping exercises (having trained evaluators go through the sales process for specific products) to verify that benefit illustrations, disclosures, and suitability assessments are actually delivered as designed.

3. Public product performance register: NAICOM to publish annual product comparison data: lapse rates, claims rates, average surrender values at years 3 and 5. This consumer-facing transparency would create competitive pressure for quality that the approval regime alone cannot generate.

4. Regulatory sandbox for innovation: A fast-track approval pathway for genuinely novel product designs (embedded microinsurance, parametric products, behaviour-linked pricing) that cannot be assessed through the standard 30-day framework.

questions.stem: 'High lapse rates in the early years of a life insurance policy are simultaneously a symptom of poor product design, a consequence of inadequate customer suitability assessment, and a driver of insurer unprofitability.' Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to the Nigerian life insurance market. In your answer, discuss the actuarial treatment of lapse assumptions in product pricing, the commercial consequences of materially adverse lapse experience, and the product design and distribution practices that can reduce early-year lapses in the Nigerian context.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is correct on all three counts but risks presenting the three causes as separate, when they are in reality deeply interconnected in the Nigerian market. High early lapse rates are a systemic problem whose roots lie simultaneously in product economics, sales culture, and actuarial risk, and they are the primary mechanism through which the Nigerian life insurance industry's profitability crisis and its trust deficit reinforce each other.
Symptom of Poor Product Design

A product that consistently generates high early lapse rates is, by definition, one that many policyholders cannot sustain. The money-back policy, the dominant Nigerian retail life product, is designed for middle-income policyholders with stable formal sector income. When it is sold to lower-income consumers or informal sector workers whose income is volatile, the design mismatch between the required premium commitment and the buyer's actual income stability is the structural cause of early lapse.

Product design flaws that drive Nigerian lapse rates:
• High premium levels relative to disposable income: Many Nigerian money-back policies are sold at premium-to-income ratios that leave no margin for unexpected income shocks.
• No premium holiday provisions: When income is temporarily disrupted, the policyholder has no in-built mechanism to pause premiums without triggering lapse.
• Front-loaded commission structures: Agents receive most of their commission in year 1, creating an incentive to prioritise sale completion over long-term policy sustainability. A policy that lapses in year 2 has already generated most of its commission income for the agent.
Consequence of Inadequate Suitability Assessment

NIIRA 2025's TCF framework requires that insurance products are sold only to consumers for whom they are suitable. In practice, pre-NIIRA 2025 Nigerian insurance sales involved minimal suitability assessment, agents documented income declarations but rarely conducted genuine affordability analysis or matched product complexity to customer financial literacy.

The suitability failure chain: An agent sells a ₦120,000 annual premium money-back policy to a customer earning ₦180,000 a year. The 67% premium-to-income ratio is obviously unsustainable through any income disruption. No suitability analysis was conducted, or if it was, it was overridden by the agent's commission incentive. The customer lapses in year 2, having paid ₦120,000 (or ₦240,000 for two years) and receiving a negligible surrender value. The customer concludes 'insurance eats money.' The trust deficit deepens.
Driver of Insurer Unprofitability

Actuarial mechanism: Life insurance pricing assumes a certain persistency pattern; that most policyholders will maintain premiums for many years, recovering the insurer's high year-1 acquisition costs through years 2–15 of premium income. When actual lapse rates materially exceed the pricing assumption:
• Year-1 acquisition costs (commission, policy set-up) are incurred for policies that terminate in year 2 without generating sufficient total premium to cover those costs.
• Reserves held for the in-force portfolio are released as policies lapse, releasing reserve strains but also eliminating future premium income.
• The portfolio's average age increases (only long-term policies remain), potentially increasing average mortality costs.
• If the product was priced at an IRR of 18% assuming 10% second-year lapse, but actual second-year lapse is 25%, the actual IRR may fall to 8–10%, below the cost of capital.
Policy Design and Distribution Reforms Required

1. Premium affordability stress testing as a suitability requirement: Before issuing a life policy, the insurer or distributor must complete a documented affordability assessment demonstrating that the annual premium does not exceed a defined percentage of verified annual income.

2. Flexible premium products: Introduce products with defined premium holiday provisions (e.g., up to 3 months per year without lapse) that match the income volatility of informal sector and gig economy customers.

3. Agent remuneration reform: Commission clawback provisions that require agents to repay a portion of first-year commission if a policy lapses within 24 months create a direct financial incentive for agents to assess suitability.

4. Conservation investment: Proactive lapse management (identifying high-risk policyholders early [through lapse propensity models, Chapter 31] and intervening with conservation offers) reduces lapse rates and is more cost-effective than writing replacement business.
